html:
A mass choral festival first held in Tartu in 1869, now held in Tallinn about every five years, where tens of thousands of singers perform together before a huge crowd.

In 1869 Estonia was part of the Russian Empire, and its towns and lands were run by a German speaking upper class. Estonians were mostly peasants who had only recently been freed from serfdom. The first festival, organised by the journalist Johann Voldemar Jannsen, brought about a thousand singers from village choirs and showed that Estonian could be a language of culture. It became a centre of the national awakening.

Under Soviet rule after 1944 the festivals went on, with Soviet songs required. But choirs also sang Estonian songs that the authorities could not stop, and singing became a way to hold the nation together. In 1988 hundreds of thousands gathered at the Tallinn song festival grounds to sing banned national songs. The protests became known as the Singing Revolution and led to independence in 1991, as the Soviet Union broke up. UNESCO honours the Baltic song festivals as world heritage.
sum: A mass choral festival first held in Tartu in 1869, now held in Tallinn about every five years, where tens of thousands of singers perform together before a huge crowd.
